items.question: In which type of output is a completeness gap most likely to go undetected during review?

options.A: Structured outputs with defined sections, because missing sections are immediately visible in the template.
options.B: Short outputs, because reviewers read them quickly without checking against the original brief.
options.C: Numeric or tabular outputs, because every cell in the expected structure is either populated or visibly empty.
options.D: Dense prose outputs, where the fluent narrative can mask the absence of required analytical elements.

items.question: Which TWO are common failure modes when evaluating Claude output for bias? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Limiting the review to explicit mentions of demographic groups, missing bias embedded in coverage depth or framing.
options.B: Applying a rubric to the output before verifying that its factual claims are accurate.
options.C: Confusing inclusive language compliance with a complete bias review, leaving coverage asymmetry unexamined.
options.D: Reviewing the output before the prompt that generated it has been reviewed for bias-inducing framing.
options.E: Using a golden set of outputs that was curated without including examples from high-stakes use cases.

items.question: What happens to reviewer consistency when a rubric is applied without a golden set for calibration?

options.A: Different reviewers may interpret the same rubric level descriptions differently, producing inconsistent scores across reviewers and over time.
options.B: The rubric becomes invalid because its dimensions cannot be scored without reference examples.
options.C: Reviewers over-rely on acceptance criteria instead of the rubric, reducing the granularity of quality measurement.
options.D: Scores drift upward over time because reviewers apply the highest rubric level to all outputs they find generally acceptable.

items.question: What is the primary risk of iterating on a fundamentally flawed output rather than rejecting and restarting?

options.A: Iterative refinement increases token costs beyond what a single high-quality generation would require.
options.B: The rubric scores for iteratively refined outputs may be inflated because reviewers become anchored to the original output.
options.C: Surface-level edits on a structurally wrong output produce an output that appears improved but retains the core defect, masking the problem from downstream users.
options.D: Iterative refinement trains the model to expect correction rather than to produce high-quality output on the first attempt.

items.question: What is the distinction between over-calibration and under-calibration as confidence-expression failure modes?

options.A: Over-calibration means expressing higher certainty than the evidence warrants; under-calibration means expressing lower certainty than the evidence warrants.
options.B: Over-calibration is a failure mode only in probabilistic or numeric claim types; under-calibration affects all output types.
options.C: Under-calibration is more harmful than over-calibration because readers are more likely to catch uncertain claims than overconfident ones.
options.D: Over-calibration and under-calibration are not distinct failure modes; both simply represent poor calibration without meaningful direction.

items.question: How can a reviewer detect sycophancy in a multi-turn conversation when each individual turn appears internally coherent?

options.A: By checking whether the final recommendation is consistent with the conclusions of external research on the same topic.
options.B: By comparing the length of each turn — sycophantic turns tend to be shorter because the model reduces reasoning effort.
options.C: By checking whether the model applied a self-consistency check before reversing its earlier position.
options.D: By tracing what information entered the conversation between each position change and whether it constitutes a valid argument for the new position.

items.question: Which TWO correctly describe consequences of using a stale golden set in output evaluation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Outputs that meet current requirements but differ in style from the old golden examples may be incorrectly flagged as low quality.
options.B: The model's training data becomes outdated, causing it to generate outputs that no longer reflect current facts.
options.C: Reviewer calibration anchors to outdated examples, causing reviewers to accept outputs that would fail current standards.
options.D: Quality regressions that matter under the current standard may go undetected because the old golden standard does not capture them.
options.E: Stale golden sets increase the cost of each review cycle because reviewers must spend more time reconciling old and new standards.

items.question: Why does rubric gaming undermine evaluation validity even when rubric scores improve?

options.A: Rubric gaming is detected by automated validators that reject inflated scores before they influence quality metrics.
options.B: Improving scores by optimizing for the rubric's measured dimensions breaks the assumed correlation between rubric scores and actual output quality for the intended use.
options.C: Rubric gaming causes reviewers to apply higher scores than the rubric level descriptions warrant, inflating the scale.
options.D: Rubric scores that improve through gaming are statistically unreliable and will revert to baseline on subsequent evaluation runs.

items.question: What distinguishes a completeness gap from an omission error in the context of high-stakes output review?

options.A: A completeness gap is a formatting problem; an omission error is a content problem.
options.B: Omission errors can be detected by the model through self-critique; completeness gaps require external reviewer verification.
options.C: A completeness gap is the absence of a required element relative to the task specification; an omission error is the absence of a fact or claim that a complete treatment of the topic would typically include.
options.D: Completeness gaps and omission errors are equivalent terms for the same failure, used interchangeably in different quality frameworks.

items.question: Which TWO correctly describe compound error propagation in Claude output? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Compound errors are always detectable by self-consistency checks because each dependent step's error must contradict the steps that follow.
options.B: A wrong intermediate result can propagate through subsequent steps, producing a final answer that is further from correct than the original error alone would predict.
options.C: Compound errors are especially dangerous because the surrounding narrative may remain logically coherent while the numeric or factual chain is systematically wrong.
options.D: Compound errors only occur in arithmetic calculations; factual or reasoning errors do not propagate across steps.
options.E: Verifying the final answer is sufficient to catch compound errors, since the cumulative effect of intermediate errors is always reflected in the final result.

items.question: Which TWO correctly explain why over-permissive acceptance criteria are particularly dangerous in high-volume workflows? (Choose TWO)

options.A: At high volume, the number of substandard outputs that pass review becomes large in absolute terms even if the per-output failure rate appears small.
options.B: High-volume workflows always involve high-stakes decisions, making any quality failure more consequential.
options.C: Human reviewers in high-volume workflows may reduce per-output review time to meet throughput targets, amplifying the risk that permissive criteria let through errors reviewers would otherwise catch.
options.D: Over-permissive criteria are more damaging at high volume because they cause the model to lower its own quality standards over subsequent generations.
options.E: High-volume workflows eliminate the possibility of escalation, meaning every output must meet the acceptance criterion without exception.

items.question: Which two activities together constitute a complete first-pass review of Claude output for reasoning quality?

options.A: Tone compliance check and application of acceptance criteria.
options.B: Factual claim verification and golden set comparison.
options.C: A self-consistency check and an arithmetic verification pass.
options.D: Prompt clarity review and output length check against requirements.

items.question: Why are a rubric and acceptance criteria complementary rather than redundant evaluation tools?

options.A: A rubric is defined before generation; acceptance criteria are defined after reviewing the output.
options.B: A rubric provides scored quality dimensions for diagnosing where quality fails; acceptance criteria provide a binary approval decision for downstream use.
options.C: Rubrics apply only to high-stakes outputs; acceptance criteria apply to all outputs regardless of stakes.
options.D: A rubric scores all quality dimensions; acceptance criteria check only the single most critical dimension.

items.question: What condition must hold for a 'good enough for purpose' acceptance standard to be justified?

options.A: A downstream human review step must exist before the output informs any consequential action.
options.B: The output must have passed through at least two rounds of iterative refinement before reaching its current form.
options.C: The model tier used must be the highest available for this class of task.
options.D: The acceptance criteria must have been independently validated against a golden set before application.

items.question: When calibration failure and a completeness gap co-occur in the same output, how should a reviewer prioritize them?

options.A: Address calibration failure first because overconfident claims mislead readers immediately, while missing sections are noticed before the output is used.
options.B: Address the completeness gap first because missing required elements affect all downstream uses equally, while calibration can be corrected by a reader applying appropriate skepticism.
options.C: Apply the organization's fixed priority order defined in the quality rubric, regardless of the specific defects present.
options.D: Assess which defect poses greater risk given the specific downstream use, rather than applying a universal priority.

items.question: How does a rubric dimension for 'logical coherence' relate to asking Claude to critique its own output?

options.A: Both target internal reasoning integrity — the rubric scores it on a defined scale while the self-critique identifies specific contradictions — making them complementary tools for the same property.
options.B: A high rubric score on logical coherence eliminates the need for a separate self-consistency check.
options.C: The self-critique provides the data needed to assign the rubric's coherence dimension score accurately.
options.D: A rubric coherence score measures external validity; a self-critique check measures internal validity.

items.question: In what way does sycophancy degrade output consistency across conversation turns?

options.A: Sycophancy improves surface consistency because the model converges on the user's preferred position across turns, reducing apparent variation.
options.B: Sycophancy degrades consistency only when the user explicitly asks the model to change its position.
options.C: Sycophancy produces cross-turn contradictions because positions shift in response to social pressure rather than new evidence, creating reversals without a principled basis.
options.D: Sycophancy affects only tone consistency, not the substantive positions the model takes across turns.

items.question: When should both a bias review and a heightened stakes-based acceptance threshold be applied to the same output?

options.A: Only when the output explicitly discusses a regulated industry such as healthcare or financial services.
options.B: Only when the model tier used is lower than the organizational standard for the task class.
options.C: Whenever the output length exceeds the typical range for this task type, since longer outputs have more opportunity for both bias and quality failures.
options.D: When the output will inform a decision about people or groups and the consequences of error are consequential for those affected.

items.question: What does a golden set contribute to output evaluation that a rubric alone cannot provide?

options.A: Concrete reference examples of what high quality looks like in practice, anchoring the rubric's abstract level descriptions to real outputs rather than verbal definitions alone.
options.B: A definitive pass/fail threshold for each dimension the rubric measures.
options.C: Automated scoring capability that reduces dependence on human reviewer judgment.
options.D: A historical record of quality scores across all previously reviewed outputs for trend analysis.

items.question: How do arithmetic verification and self-critique complement each other as output review techniques?

options.A: Self-critique replaces arithmetic verification for outputs that do not contain numeric claims.
options.B: Both detect the same errors, so applying one eliminates the need for the other in most review workflows.
options.C: Arithmetic verification catches computational errors through independent recalculation; self-critique catches logical gaps and contradictions through a second reasoning pass — targeting distinct failure modes.
options.D: Arithmetic verification must always precede self-critique because computational errors propagate into reasoning errors that the self-critique would then incorrectly validate.

items.question: How does output calibration quality affect the efficiency of a reviewer's acceptance decision?

options.A: A well-calibrated output automatically passes acceptance criteria because calibration quality is equivalent to overall output quality.
options.B: A poorly calibrated output automatically fails acceptance criteria because miscalibrated confidence is a disqualifying defect in all use cases.
options.C: Calibration quality is assessed in a separate workflow and does not interact with the acceptance decision process.
options.D: A well-calibrated output directs reviewer attention toward claims that actually warrant scrutiny, making the acceptance review more efficient than reviewing an uncalibrated output requires.

items.question: Which TWO evaluation tools together provide both a scored quality framework and a concrete reference standard for consistent output review? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Acceptance criteria
options.B: Evaluation rubric
options.C: Completeness checklist
options.D: Golden set

items.question: How does the stakes level of an output's downstream use affect the tolerance for a completeness gap?

options.A: Higher stakes narrow the tolerance — a gap acceptable in a low-stakes draft may disqualify an output from high-stakes use.
options.B: Stakes level and completeness gaps are assessed through separate review activities that do not influence each other.
options.C: Any completeness gap automatically triggers escalation to a domain expert regardless of the stakes level.
options.D: Completeness gaps only affect acceptance decisions when they are explicitly listed as a rubric dimension.

items.question: What happens to evaluation validity when acceptance criteria are set more strictly than the output's intended use requires?

options.A: Over-strict criteria systematically reject outputs that would have met the downstream need, creating unnecessary rework while providing no quality benefit above what the use case actually demands.
options.B: Over-strict criteria improve quality by ensuring only the highest-quality outputs reach downstream use, always benefiting the audience.
options.C: Over-strict criteria have no effect on output quality outcomes but increase token and review costs unnecessarily.
options.D: Over-strict criteria are always preferable to over-permissive criteria because they err on the side of caution.

items.question: Why cannot a rubric score alone determine whether sycophancy affected an output's reasoning quality?

options.A: Rubrics rarely include a logical coherence dimension, so sycophantic reasoning goes unscored.
options.B: Rubric scoring is inherently too subjective to detect behavioral phenomena like sycophancy reliably.
options.C: Sycophancy is a behavioral pattern that requires comparing the output to the conversational context that preceded it — a rubric assesses the output in isolation and cannot evaluate the mechanism that produced the position.
options.D: Rubric dimensions can only assess content quality, not the process by which content was generated.

items.question: What is the key distinction between a calibration failure and an acceptance criteria failure in output quality review?

options.A: Calibration failures are detected through rubric scoring; acceptance criteria failures are detected through pass/fail evaluation.
options.B: A calibration failure concerns how confidently claims are expressed relative to their reliability; an acceptance criteria failure concerns whether the output meets the quality threshold required for approved use.
options.C: An acceptance criteria failure always implies a calibration failure because outputs that fail quality thresholds must contain miscalibrated confidence.
options.D: Calibration failures are always more serious than acceptance criteria failures because they mislead reviewers about which claims to scrutinize.

items.question: How can a golden set be used to identify whether current acceptance criteria are too permissive?

options.A: If golden examples frequently fail the current acceptance criteria, those criteria are too permissive.
options.B: By comparing outputs that have passed acceptance criteria to golden examples — if passing outputs are systematically weaker than golden reference quality, the criteria permit quality levels below what the golden set endorses as adequate.
options.C: By calculating the average rubric score of all golden examples and using it to reset the acceptance threshold.
options.D: By running the golden inputs through the current prompt and checking whether they produce outputs similar to the golden examples.

items.question: Which TWO conditions together most strongly justify both conducting a bias review AND escalating the output for expert sign-off? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The output required more than three iterative refinement cycles to reach its current form.
options.B: The output will be used to inform a consequential decision about specific individuals or groups.
options.C: The primary reviewer lacks sufficient domain expertise to assess whether the bias review findings are materially significant.
options.D: The output's tone deviates marginally from the brand voice guidelines.
options.E: The output was generated using a lower model tier than the organizational standard recommends for this task class.

items.question: In which case do overconfident tone and hallucination diverge as distinct rather than overlapping failure modes?

options.A: They always overlap because the training dynamics that produce hallucination also systematically suppress appropriate hedging.
options.B: They are distinct whenever they occur in different sections of the same output.
options.C: They overlap when a false claim is stated without hedging; they are distinct when a true claim is overstated or a false claim is appropriately hedged.
options.D: They diverge when a factually accurate claim is stated with excessive certainty — overconfident tone without hallucination — or when a fabricated claim is presented with appropriate uncertainty — hallucination without overconfident tone.

items.question: Which TWO quality properties remain unverified when both self-consistency checking and external verification are omitted from a high-stakes output review? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Internal logical coherence — whether the output's claims are consistent with each other within the same document.
options.B: Format compliance — whether the output follows the structural requirements specified in the prompt.
options.C: External factual accuracy — whether the output's claims correspond to authoritative sources outside the output.
options.D: Tone compliance — whether the output's register and voice match the brand specifications.
options.E: Length appropriateness — whether the output falls within the specified word count range.

items.question: Which TWO correctly identify how rubric gaming and sycophancy both undermine evaluation integrity through analogous mechanisms? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Both decouple an observed quality signal from what it is supposed to measure: rubric scores decouple from actual output usefulness; sycophantic positions decouple from evidence-based reasoning.
options.B: Both arise from training data deficiencies in the specific task domain.
options.C: Both can be detected by automated tools that flag when scores or positions change without accompanying changes in the underlying evidence.
options.D: Both create a surface appearance of quality — high rubric scores or well-supported-seeming positions — that does not reflect the actual quality of the underlying content or reasoning.
options.E: Both can be fully resolved by escalating to a higher model tier, which resists optimization pressure and social influence.

options.B: When latency constraints on the workflow are relaxed
options.C: When the prompt has not yet been revised or refined

options.A: The model allocates additional computation to explore reasoning paths before producing its final answer
options.B: The model is able to access a larger context window
options.C: The model returns a shorter, more precise response by default
options.D: The model bypasses its standard output-safety evaluation

options.D: Connectors replace Project knowledge entirely

options.B: Allow multiple users to share one live context window simultaneously
options.C: Require API access to create and manage

options.B: Switch to a mixed-tier pipeline and assign Haiku to shallow steps
options.C: Revise the prompt to explicitly specify depth, structure, and success criteria

options.B: Context-window size and reasoning depth are always equivalent across tiers
options.C: Only API users encounter context-window limits in practice
options.D: Exceeding the context window automatically routes the request to a higher-tier model

options.C: The final synthesis step that produces the client-facing deliverable
options.D: Steps that use extended thinking to explore reasoning paths
